title: Where a vLLM cold start goes
question: Where does a cold [vLLM](p1:vllm) start on a rented GPU spend its time, and which empty cache is worth warming more: the weights or the [compiled GPU code](p1:compile)? One also bought serving memory ([KV cache](p1:kvcache)).

requirements.text: Split one [cold start](p1:coldstart) into named phases, and label time that cannot be attributed instead of hiding it.
requirements.why: The caches act on different phases ([weights](p1:weights) on loading, [compile](p1:compile) on engine start), so one "startup" bar would hide half the experiment.

requirements.text: Any two set-ups compared differ only in cache configuration: same image, entrypoint and engine flags.
requirements.why: Otherwise a difference cannot be pinned on a cache.

requirements.text: Report each arm's spread as percentiles, and give every comparison its own interval.
requirements.why: Cold starts are skewed with a heavy tail, so a mean describes no real run. "Cache X matters more" needs its own interval, not two point estimates side by side.

requirements.text: Commit the hypotheses, which runs get thrown out, when to stop and how the headline is chosen, before the first paid measurement run.
requirements.why: Git timestamps then show the rules came before the data, and the headline cannot be picked by which result cost the most effort.

requirements.text: Run on paid GPUs only code already tested offline, and let anyone re-derive every number on a laptop.
requirements.why: The whole budget was $200, and debugging on live GPUs eats it. A number a reader cannot re-derive must be taken on trust.
requirements.unlinked_reason: It is met by process: the flow step "Capture, then build offline" tests the code on recorded logs, API responses and a free fake engine before paid runs, and "Publish what re-derives" re-derives every figure with no GPU.

concepts.plain: Three cache set-ups. **A**: weights from the model hub, [compile cache](p1:compile) cold. **B**: weights from a network volume, compile cache cold. **C**: weights from the volume, compile cache warm.
One run of each arm, in an order shuffled from a seed. 100 triples make the 300 runs, so a busy hour on the rented GPUs falls on all three arms.

A **contrast** is the difference of two arms' medians, with a 95% bootstrap interval (resample the runs 10,000 times, keep the middle 95%): A minus B is the weight cache's saving, B minus C the compile cache's. Their **difference**, (A minus B) minus (B minus C), ranks the caches only if its interval excludes zero; negative favours the compile cache.

concepts.term: Two clocks and the platform residual
concepts.plain: **Clock A** (laptop) brackets the whole job; total [cold start](p1:coldstart) is its span minus the worker-clock warmup after the first request. **Clock B** (worker) starts just before `vllm serve` is launched. **Platform time** = total minus clock B time, the one allowed cross-clock subtraction: queue, container start, handler set-up, teardown, polling lag.
**p90** is the time 90% of runs finish within; p50 is the median. An **ECDF** plots every run (seconds across, share finished up), so the tail stays visible.

**H1**: weight handling is over half of worker-clock time through the first request in arm A. **H2**: volume weights cut it materially. **H3**: compiling is a non-trivial part of engine start, and a warm cache cuts it. **H4**: host differences drive how far p95 sits above the median. **H5**: a warm compile cache leaves more [KV cache](p1:kvcache).

Hypotheses, contrasts, which runs to throw out, when to stop and how to pick the headline, committed in `docs/experiment.md` before any paid measurement run, four days before the published campaign's first run; later additions are dated in git.

decisions.title: Three arms, one variable
decisions.problem: Two caches start empty: the weights and the compiled code. To rank them, each comparison must change one thing only.
options: Two arms: hub vs volume weights
Add a baked-image arm, weights inside the container image
Add the fourth cell: weights cold, compile cache warm
One variable, cache configuration, at three levels: A, B, C
decisions.chosen: One variable, cache configuration, at three levels: A, B, C
decisions.why: A to B isolates the weight cache. B to C isolates the compile cache with weight handling held constant. The configuration is one frozen object that sets two paths, so the single-variable claim is true by structure. A baked image only moves the bytes into the image pull, inside the platform residual the harness cannot split, so it would flatter the weight time unseen. Nobody warms a compile cache while re-downloading weights, so the fourth cell answers no question.
decisions.cost: Arm C exists only because a trial run before measuring showed this vLLM compiles at startup. A warm arm needs a primed volume, and a test has to check that the arms differ nowhere else.
decisions.why_short: A to B isolates the weight cache, B to C the compile cache; one frozen configuration makes the single-variable claim true by structure.
decisions.cost_short: Arm C needs a primed volume, and a test checks that the arms differ nowhere else.

serves.because: One frozen configuration sets both cache paths, so each arm differs from the next in exactly one thing.

uses.because: Three arms give each cache its own one-step comparison: A to B for weights, B to C for compile.
Each adjacent pair of arms yields one contrast, so each cache's saving is measured on its own.

decisions.title: Measure from outside the engine
decisions.problem: vLLM's interesting phases are internal, and part of every cold start (queue, container start, image pull) happens before our code exists.
options: Time startup through vLLM's Python engine API
One clock, and give all the time to the stages you can see
Run the real `vllm serve`, bracket it with a worker clock, split phases from its log, and get platform time by subtraction
decisions.chosen: Run the real `vllm serve`, bracket it with a worker clock, split phases from its log, and get platform time by subtraction
decisions.why: The Python API would measure a startup path nobody deploys. With one clock you cannot detect that it is lying; the implemented check compares the laptop and worker clocks and discards a run whose total leaves no room for a network round trip.
decisions.cost: Platform time is one residual holding teardown and polling lag as well as queueing. RunPod's queue and execution durations (clock C) are recorded but not used to split it. Two engine sub-phases (device init and KV allocation) are not delineated by this vLLM build, so they sit merged in an unattributed row. The log patterns are tied to vLLM 0.27.1.
decisions.why_short: Timing the real `vllm serve` from outside measures the path people deploy, and a second clock lets a lying run be caught.
decisions.cost_short: Platform time is one residual that also holds teardown and polling lag; two engine sub-phases stay merged.

serves.because: Engine phases come from vLLM's own log; what it cannot split goes in a labelled unattributed row and a named platform residual, so nothing is hidden.

uses.because: Two clocks let platform time be found by subtraction, and let a run whose clocks disagree be caught.

decisions.title: Interleave the arms in random triples
decisions.problem: Conditions on rented GPUs change over hours and days. Run the arms in blocks and a busy evening gets labelled as an arm effect.
options: Blocks: all of A, then all of B, then all of C
Interleaved triples: one run of each arm per triple, order shuffled from a seed
decisions.chosen: Interleaved triples: one run of each arm per triple, order shuffled from a seed
decisions.why: Blocking confounds the cache with time-of-day conditions, and on rented GPUs that confound can be large enough to make or erase the whole effect. The design calls interleaving its most important validity decision. Triples also allow a paired, same-host check as supporting evidence.
decisions.cost: A resumed campaign must rebuild the exact schedule, so the harness refuses a resume whose stored arms disagree with the seed. The windows ended up hours apart rather than on separate days, so drift between windows is only partly covered; the post says so.
decisions.why_short: Running all of one arm first would mix the cache effect with time-of-day conditions on the platform.
decisions.cost_short: A resume must rebuild the exact schedule; drift between windows hours apart is only partly covered.

serves.because: In blocks, the time of day changes along with the arm, so a busy evening would pose as an arm effect.

uses.because: Each triple puts all three arms in the same stretch of time, so drift lands on every arm alike.

decisions.title: Check each arm's cache state
decisions.problem: A warm cache leaking into a cold arm, or a cold compile inside arm C, would still produce plausible numbers. The configuration alone does not show what was on disk.
options: Let arm C's first campaign runs warm the cache
Prime arm C outside the campaign, isolate cold paths per run, and check the compile-cache state on every run
decisions.chosen: Prime arm C outside the campaign, isolate cold paths per run, and check the compile-cache state on every run
decisions.why: Without priming, arm C's early runs compile cold and later ones do not: a mixture whose effect grows with run index, which looks like a real trend. So two priming runs go to a separate store, and the second must show the cache present and compile under one second. Cold paths are named by run id so a reused worker cannot hand one run's files to another. The cache state is checked before the engine starts, since a cold compile creates the directory as it finishes; a run whose state disagrees with its arm is discarded.
decisions.cost: Priming runs cost GPU time and are excluded from every number. Moving the check to after the engine run would look harmless but quietly discard about two thirds of a paid campaign, so the code carries a do-not-move warning.
decisions.why_short: Unprimed, arm C's early runs compile cold and later ones do not, which looks like a real trend.
decisions.cost_short: Priming runs cost GPU time and are excluded from every number.

serves.because: A leaked warm cache, or a cold compile in arm C, would make the arms differ in more than their configured cache, and the configuration alone does not show what was on disk.

uses.because: Each arm has an expected cache state, so a run whose observed state disagrees can be caught and discarded.

decisions.title: Rank the caches by the difference's interval
decisions.problem: Which cache buys more? Two effects, each with its own interval, do not answer that.
options: Subtract the weight-time contrast from the compile-time contrast
Bootstrap the difference of contrasts on total cold start, and pick the headline by a rule fixed in advance
decisions.chosen: Bootstrap the difference of contrasts on total cold start, and pick the headline by a rule fixed in advance
decisions.why: "Compile cache mattered more" is only a finding if the gap between the two effects excludes zero. The difference needs one shared unit, so it is computed on total cold start; subtracting weight time from compile time would difference two different quantities. The headline rule, lead with what transfers furthest to other infrastructure, was committed before data.
decisions.cost: Total time is noisier than the mechanism units, so the interval is wide: −10.39 s, 95% [−20.30, −5.54]. The pre-registration requires it reported before any ranking claim.
decisions.why_short: "Compile cache mattered more" is a finding only if the gap between the two effects excludes zero.
decisions.cost_short: Total time is noisy, so the interval is wide and the ranking claim must always carry it.

serves.because: Two savings side by side do not rank the caches; only an interval on their difference can.
Leading with what transfers furthest, a rule committed before data, stops the headline being picked afterwards.

uses.because: The ranking is the difference of the two contrasts.
The pre-registration requires the difference's interval before any ranking claim, so the claim never appears without it.

decisions.title: Report the shape, and what it cannot answer
decisions.problem: Cold starts have a heavy right tail, and 100 runs per arm cannot support every summary.
options: Drop the host hypothesis (H4) quietly once every run lands on one host
p50, p90, p95 and a full ECDF, no p99, and H4 reported as unanswerable
decisions.chosen: p50, p90, p95 and a full ECDF, no p99, and H4 reported as unanswerable
decisions.why: A mean is pulled by the tail. At 100 runs a p99 is one or two observations, not an estimate. Before the published campaign began (a discarded window had already shown runs piling onto one host), the pre-registration committed to publishing the host count whatever it was. The same single host made every triple host-complete, so the paired check is fully supplied.
decisions.cost: The far tail stays unresolved: the post can say that B's largest repeat-host runs were longer than A's, but not why. The question of whether host placement drives the tail is lost.
decisions.why_short: A mean hides the tail, and at 100 runs a p99 would be one or two observations.
decisions.cost_short: The far tail stays unresolved, and whether host placement drives it is unanswered.
decisions.short: Report the shape and its limits

serves.because: A mean is pulled by the tail, so percentiles and the full ECDF describe real runs instead.
H4 was fixed in advance, so it is reported as unanswerable instead of quietly dropped.

uses.because: p50 to p95 hold up at 100 runs per arm; a p99 would be one or two runs.
H4 asked whether host placement drives the tail, and one host cannot answer it.

flow.label: Capture, then build offline
flow.detail: Real vLLM logs and RunPod responses from a cheap trial run are saved as test inputs; the code is tested on them and on a free fake engine. A disk-fill defect still cost one discarded 27-run window.

flow.label: Pre-register
flow.detail: Hypotheses, contrasts and rules are committed in `docs/experiment.md` before the first paid measurement run.

flow.label: Prime arm C
flow.detail: Two arm C runs go to a separate store and never count; the second must show compile under one second. Each run checks its compile cache before the engine starts, because a cold compile creates it as it finishes.

flow.label: Run interleaved triples
flow.detail: 100 seeded triples, one job in flight. Any change to a pinned setting ends the experiment.

flow.label: Store, never retry
flow.detail: One JSON line per run, appended as it lands. A failure is its own row, never retried: a retry would swap slow or unlucky runs for faster ones.

flow.label: Partition, then analyse
flow.detail: A gate sorts rows into publishable, discarded and failed before any statistic; then seeded bootstrap intervals (10,000 iterations).

flow.label: Publish what re-derives
flow.detail: Figures and the post come from the committed store; a re-run reproduces the analysis byte for byte, with no GPU.

results.title: Where each arm's median cold start goes

deltas.text: Weight cache only: launch to model loaded falls 45.83 → 30.35 s; compile stays near 19 s.
Compile cache only: compile falls 18.79 → 0.33 s. Launch to model loaded also falls, 30.35 → 21.34 s, unexplained.

results.axis: Median seconds per phase, 100 runs per arm. A: nothing cached; B: weights cached; C: both cached. Compile is drawn last, out of time order (it follows model loading). Unattributed engine start: two sub-phases the log does not split. Other fixed steps: [memory profiling](p1:vllm), [graph capture](p1:compile), the ready check (engine up until health answers, mostly API-server start-up), the first request, start to finish.
results.read_as: The launch segment runs from starting `vllm serve` to its "Model loading took" line, so it holds process start-up too; vLLM's own loading time is 17.40, 4.57, 4.54 s. Dashed box on C: B's compile time.
results.takeaway: Each cache shrinks the phase it acts on: weights the launch segment, compile the compile segment. One segment moved that should not have: C also reaches "model loaded" sooner than B.
results.arithmetic: Each segment is one phase's median over 100 runs; Other fixed steps adds four such medians (A: 8.82 s), so it is not itself a median, and bars miss the median totals (81.12, 65.43, 39.37 s).

results.title: How spread out the runs are

chart.note: Hollow circle: the arm's largest repeat-host run; the post gives it for A and B only.

results.axis: Seconds of total cold start per arm: p50 (median), p90, p95.
results.read_as: The arm order holds at every percentile shown, but among repeat-host runs B's largest is longer than A's: the far tail does not follow the median. No p99: at 100 runs it would be one or two runs.
results.arithmetic: Percentiles use all 300 publishable runs, among them arm A's 2266.6 s run on a host's first image pull (far past p95); each hollow marker is that arm's largest repeat-host run (A: 99 runs, B: 100).
results.takeaway: The ranking holds out to p95, yet among repeat-host runs B's largest exceeds A's: the far tail is not the median.

results.title: The two effects, each measured on its own
results.axis: Seconds of total cold start each cache saves (median difference), with a 95% bootstrap interval.
results.read_as: Both clear zero, but side by side they do not rank the caches; the next chart does. Only 18.46 s of the compile cache's 26.07 s is compilation; the other 7.6 s roughly matches the unexplained launch-segment gap (8.85 s).
results.takeaway: Each cache saves time on its own, and neither interval comes near zero; these are context, not the ranking.
results.arithmetic: A − B and B − C use unrounded medians, so 15.68 and 26.07 s, not the 15.69 and 26.06 the rounded medians (81.12, 65.43, 39.37) give.

results.title: Which cache bought more: the interval on the difference
results.axis: Weight-cache saving minus compile-cache saving: seconds of total cold start, 95% bootstrap interval.
results.read_as: The whole interval, −20.30 to −5.54 s, lies left of zero, which licenses the ranking; the pre-registration requires this interval before any ranking claim.
results.takeaway: The compile cache saves more, about 10 s per cold start, and the interval never crosses zero, so the ranking is a finding, not a reading of two bars.
results.arithmetic: 15.68 − 26.07 = −10.39 s (contrasts use unrounded medians, so they differ from differences of the rounded totals 81.12, 65.43, 39.37 s); the interval comes from 10,000 resamples of the runs.

results.title: KV cache left for serving, by arm
results.axis: KV cache tokens vLLM allocated at startup, same card and flags in every arm.
results.read_as: C keeps 20.3 % more KV cache: one more full-length (8192-token) request served at once, 5 instead of 4. On a cold arm the compiler's working set is resident while vLLM measures free memory, so the cache is sized smaller for the replica's life. Pre-registered as H5.
results.takeaway: B and C differ only in the compile cache, yet C gets 20.3 % more KV cache: one more full-length request at a time, for the replica's whole life.
results.arithmetic: 43,040 / 8,192 = 5.25 and 35,792 / 8,192 = 4.37 full-length requests; the code keeps whole requests (rounds down), so 5 against 4. 43,040 / 35,792 = 1.203, so 20.3 % more.

interview.pitch30: I measured where the time goes when a vLLM server starts cold on a rented GPU, and which of two caches is worth warming: the model weights or the engine's compiled code. I ran three set-ups differing in one thing only, interleaved, a hundred times each, and split every start into phases. The compile cache saved about 10 seconds more per cold start than the weight cache, 95% interval 5.5 to 20 seconds more, and it left about 20% more KV cache for serving.
interview.pitch120: Everyone talks about caching the weights. But vLLM also compiles parts of the model at startup and caches that on disk, a cache few notice unless they have operated the engine. I set up three arms that differ only in cache configuration: nothing cached, weights on a network volume, and weights plus a warm compile cache. I ran them as shuffled triples so platform drift could not pose as an arm effect, and I committed my hypotheses and rules before the first paid measurement run. I timed the real `vllm serve` with one clock in the worker and one on my laptop, so platform start-up is a named residual, not hidden. The answer: warming the compile cache saved about 10 seconds more per cold start than caching the weights, and the interval on that difference never crossed zero. It also left about a fifth more KV cache, because profiling no longer ran next to the compiler's memory. What it cannot tell you is anything about other hardware, or whether host placement drives the tail: every run landed on one machine, and I reported that rather than dropping the question.

followups.q: Why three arms and not two, or four?
followups.a: Two arms (hub vs volume) only test the weight cache: the fallback had this vLLM not compiled at startup; it does. A to B isolates weights, B to C compile with weights fixed. The fourth cell, weights cold but compile warm, has no operational meaning. A baked-image arm would only move the bytes into the image pull, which I cannot observe.

The git timestamp is the only evidence that the hypotheses and the headline rule came before the data: they were committed four days before the published campaign's first run. Later amendments are dated, among them the rule separating a host's first image pull, written about half an hour after window one showed a 2174 s platform time. None changed a hypothesis or a contrast.

Two things. C reached "model loaded" 8.85 s sooner than B, on arms that differ only in compile cache, while vLLM's own model-loading time is the same in B and C (4.57 vs 4.54 s): not host, not position in the triple, and this campaign does not explain it. And "ready is not fast" was wrong here: [vLLM](p1:vllm) does its warmup before answering health, so the first request is already near steady state.

The host question failed: a serially-submitting driver kept landing on the one machine that had the image cached. The windows were hours apart, not separate days. And the first window was thrown out because arm A's per-run [weights](p1:weights) filled the worker disk (A failed 3 of its 9 runs, B none), which would have biased the contrast; the worker now empties cold directories before and after each run.

followups.q: What does this not tell you?
followups.a: The seconds for any other GPU, model, engine version, region or provider. Anything about many [serverless](p1:serverless) replicas starting at once and contending for the same volume; every run was one replica alone. Anything past p95. And whether host placement drives the tail.

followups.q: So should everyone warm the compile cache?
followups.a: It is the better buy and the more fragile one. A [compile cache](p1:compile) costs nothing to store, but any change to engine version, model, hardware or flags invalidates it, so every upgrade pays the cold compile again unless warming is built into the deploy. The weight cache is a volume you rent every month whether you scale or not.

interview.limits: One provider, GPU model, model, engine version, region and host: the seconds do not transfer; the mechanisms do. H4 (does host placement drive the tail?) is unanswerable: all 300 runs landed on one host. Single replica, no contention. No percentile past p95. The first-touch rule that keeps the 2266.6 s run out of the ECDF (it stays in the medians) was written after seeing the data and is disclosed as post hoc. Why C reaches "model loaded" 8.85 s sooner than B is not settled.

recall.q: B and C differ only in the compile cache. Which chart segment should change, and which other one changed?
recall.a: Only compile should move, and it does: 18.79 to 0.33 s. The launch segment also shrank, 30.35 to 21.34 s, though vLLM's own loading time is the same in B and C (4.57 vs 4.54 s). The campaign does not explain it.

recall.q: On the one-run view, where does clock B start, and what lands in platform time?
recall.a: Between steps 4 and 5: the probe starts clock B just before launching `vllm serve`. Platform time is everything the laptop clock sees outside it: queueing, finding a GPU, starting the container and handler set-up before; teardown and the driver's 5 s polling after.

recall.q: Why is arm C primed outside the campaign?
recall.a: Otherwise its early runs compile cold and its later runs do not, making the arm a mixture whose effect grows with run index and looks like a trend.

recall.q: Why is the compile cache checked before the engine starts, not after?
recall.a: A cold compile creates the cache directory as it finishes. Checked afterwards, every healthy cold run would look warm and be discarded, and a cold compile inside arm C would pass as warm.

recall.q: How is a contrast obtained, and why does the ranking need a third number?
recall.a: Subtract the medians of two arms that differ in one cache, with a bootstrap interval. Which cache saves more is a claim about the difference of the two contrasts, so it needs its own interval, on one shared unit: total cold start.

recall.q: If the difference's interval had run from −20 to +3 s, what could you claim?
recall.a: Not the ranking: no difference, or a slightly larger weight-cache saving, would still fit, and the design makes the ranking a finding only if the interval excludes zero. Each cache's own saving, with its interval, could still be reported.

recall.q: Which requirement breaks if the arms run in blocks, and what protects it?
recall.a: R2, one change per comparison: in blocks, time-of-day platform conditions change along with the cache. Interleaved triples protect it, with one frozen cache configuration and the per-run check of each arm's compile-cache state.

recall.q: Why is a failed run never retried in place?
recall.a: A retry quietly replaces slow or unlucky runs with faster ones and makes the distribution look better than it is. Failures are their own rows and are counted per arm.

recall.q: Why does the warm compile cache leave more KV cache?
recall.a: vLLM sizes the KV cache from free memory measured during a profiling pass. On a cold arm the compiler's working set is resident during that pass, so less memory looks free, and the smaller cache stays for the replica's life.
